rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people imprisoned Abraham in Kutha and built an enclosure like a pen; Abū Ḥayyān omits disputed details about its dimensions and the fire as contradictory.
rows.anchor: وروي أنهم حين هموا بإحراقه حبسوه ثم بنوا بيتا كالحظيرة بكوثى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says Iblīs taught them the catapult, which had not been made before; they bound Abraham and cast him into the fire.
rows.anchor: قيل: بتعليم إبليس إذ كان لم يصنع قبل فشد إبراهيم رباطا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gabriel asked Abraham whether he needed anything; Abraham replied that he needed nothing from Gabriel.
rows.anchor: ألك حاجة؟ فقال: أما إليك فلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Exegetes also told stories about animals’ actions during the fire, but Abū Ḥayyān says God knows their truth.
rows.anchor: من الوزغ والبغل والخطاف والضفدع والعضرفوط الله أعلم بذلك.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says Abraham was saved by saying, ‘God is sufficient for me, and He is the best disposer of affairs.’
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس: إنما نجا بقوله حسبي الله ونعم الوكيل.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says Nimrod saw Abraham in a garden with an angel, vowed to sacrifice four thousand cows to Abraham’s God, and spared him; Abraham was then sixteen.
rows.anchor: فذبح أربعة آلاف بقرة. وكف عن إبراهيم، وكان إبراهيم إذ ذاك ابن ست عشرة سنة،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān regards the Qur’an’s account as sound: Abraham was thrown into the fire, God made it cool and safe, and he emerged unharmed; this was a supreme sign.
rows.anchor: والذي صح هو ما ذكره تعالى من أنه ألقي في النار فجعلها الله عليه بردا وسلاما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent speaker of ‘We said’ is God; another view says it was Gabriel acting by God’s command.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن القائل قلنا يا نار هو الله تعالى. وقيل: جبريل عليه السلام بأمر الله تعالى.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says that without ‘and peace’ the cold would have killed Abraham, and without ‘upon Abraham’ no fire afterward would burn or kindle.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس: لو لم يقل: وسلاما لهلك إبراهيم من البرد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here salāman means safety, not a greeting: a greeting would more fittingly be nominative than accusative.
rows.anchor: ومعنى وسلاما سلامة، وأبعد من ذهب إلى أنها هنا تحية من الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The construction means ‘possessing coolness and safety’; it intensifies the sense until the fire itself is as though coolness and safety.
rows.anchor: والمعنى ذات برد وسلام فبولغ في ذلك كان ذاتها برد وسلام،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s address and command to the fire portray it as a rational listener because it responds to God’s will as a rational being would.
rows.anchor: ولما كانت النار تنفعل لما أراده الله منها كما ينفعل من يعقل

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī explains that God removed the fire’s heat and burning while leaving its light, radiance, and flame intact.
rows.anchor: نزع الله عنها طبعها الذي طبعها عليه من الحر والإحراق

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī also suggests that God protected Abraham from even slight heat and made him experience its opposite, as He does with the keepers of Hell; ‘upon Abraham’ supports this reading.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يدفع بقدرته عن جسم إبراهيم أدنى حرها ويذيقه فيها عكس ذلك كما يفعل بخزنة جهنم،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people claimed the fire would not burn, tested it on one of their elders, and saw him burn; they intended this as a plot against Abraham.
rows.anchor: وروي أنهم قالوا هي نار مسجورة لا تحرق فرموا فيها شيخا منهم فاحترق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘We made them the greatest losers’ means their loss was maximal: their plan was nullified, Abraham refuted them, and God rescued him after they seized and cast him in.
rows.anchor: قيل: هو إلقاؤه في النار فجعلناهم الأخسرين أي المبالغين في الخسران

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another report says God sent mosquitoes against the people, which ate their flesh and drank their blood, and one mosquito tormented Nimrod until he died; accounts differ on its effect and duration.
rows.anchor: وهو البعوض يأكل من لحومهم ويشرب من دمائهم،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in ‘We rescued him’ refers to Abraham; the verb takes ‘to’ because it carries the sense of bringing him safely out to the land.
rows.anchor: والضمير في ونجيناه عائد على إبراهيم وضمن معنى أخرجناه بنجاتنا إلى الأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, ‘to the land’ modifies an omitted word meaning ‘ending at the land’ and functions circumstantially, so no added sense is needed in the verb.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يكون إلى متعلقا بمحذوف أي منتهيا إلى الأرض فيكون في موضع الحال،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The land Abraham and Lot left was Kutha in Iraq; their blessed destination was Syria, known for fertility, trees, rivers, and as the birthplace of most prophets.
rows.anchor: والأرض التي خرجا منها هي كوثى من أرض العراق، والأرض التي صار إليها هي أرض الشام

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the blessed destination as Mecca, invoking the verse about the first House.
rows.anchor: وقيل: مكة قاله ابن عباس، كما قال إن أول بيت الآية.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view identifies the destination as Egypt and its blessing with the Nile, fertile crops, and flourishing settlements.
rows.anchor: وقيل أرض مصر وبركتها نيلها وزكاة زروعها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says Abraham emigrated for his Lord with his nephew Lot and cousin Sarah, who believed in him and accompanied him to preserve her faith; on the journey he met the ruler who tried to take her and stayed in Harran.
rows.anchor: فآمنت به سارة وهي ابنة عمه فأخرجها معه فارا بدينه،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view says Sarah was the daughter of Harran’s king; Abraham married her after her father stipulated that he not change her.
rows.anchor: وقيل: سارة ابنة ملك حران تزوجها إبراهيم وشرط عليه أبوها أن لا يغيرها،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān rejects the king’s-daughter account as the sound view and identifies Sarah as Abraham’s cousin, daughter of Hārān the elder.
rows.anchor: والصحيح أنها ابنة عمه هاران الأكبر،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham later went from Egypt to Syria, settling at al-Sabʿ in Palestine; Lot settled at al-Muʾtafika nearby and was sent as a prophet.
rows.anchor: ثم قدم مصر ثم خرج منها إلى الشام فنزل السبع من أرض فلسطين

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid and ʿAṭāʾ explain nāfilah as a gift.
rows.anchor: والنافلة العطية قاله مجاهد وعطاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation is an added gift: Isaac fulfilled Abraham’s prayer for righteous offspring, while Jacob was granted in addition without a separate prayer.
rows.anchor: إذا كان إسحاق ثمرة دعائه رب هب لي من الصالحين، وكان يعقوب زيادة من غير دعاء.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further view takes nāfilah to mean a grandchild, referring to Jacob; on this reading the word is circumstantial, while the gift/addition reading treats it as a verbal noun.
rows.anchor: وقيل: النافلة ولد الولد فعلى الأول يكون مصدرا كالعاقبة والعافية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Each’ includes Abraham, Lot, Isaac, and Jacob, the people just named.
rows.anchor: وكلا يشمل من ذكر إبراهيم ولوط وإسحاق ويعقوب.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prophets guided people to religion by God’s command and served as exemplary leaders for others.
rows.anchor: يهدون بأمرنا يرشدون الناس إلى الدين. وأئمة قدوة لغيرهم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘We revealed to them’ means God honored them specifically with prophethood, since revelation is the commissioning of a prophet.
rows.anchor: وأوحينا إليهم أي خصصناهم بشرف النبوة لأن الإيحاء هو التنبئة.

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī derives the verbal nouns for doing good deeds, establishing prayer, and giving alms from underlying clauses with ‘that they do.’
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: فعل الخيرات أصله أن يفعل فعل الخيرات

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī prefers a passive construction so the deeds will not appear to belong exclusively to the prophets, since other people share these obligations.
rows.anchor: بنى الفعل للمفعول حتى لا يكون المصدر مضافا من حيث المعنى إلى ضمير الموحى،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān says the omitted agent can be all legally responsible people, including followers; alternatively, the deeds can be ascribed to the prophets without implying exclusivity.
rows.anchor: ولا يلزم ذلك إذ الفاعل مع المصدر محذوف، ويجوز أن يكون مضافا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that a verbal noun can be built in the passive is disputed: al-Akhfash allows it, but the correct position forbids it, so al-Zamakhsharī’s choice is not preferred.
rows.anchor: ثم اعتقاد بناء المصدر للمفعول الذي لم يسم فاعله مختلف فيه

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya questions the form iqām as a verbal noun.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: والإقام مصدر وفي هذا نظر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān answers that Sībawayh attests iqām as a verbal noun meaning إقامة; although the latter is more common, the shortened form fits a weak-root pattern and balances it with إيتاء.
rows.anchor: وقد نص سيبويه على أنه مصدر بمعنى الإقامة، وإن كان الأكثر الإقامة بالتاء

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj says the tāʾ of iqāmat was dropped because the possessive construction compensates for it; Abū Ḥayyān calls this al-Farrāʾ’s weak position.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: فحذفت الهاء من إقامة لأن الإضافة عوض عنها انتهى.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accusative Lot is parsed as a fronted object whose governing verb is understood; the judgment given to him means prophethood.
rows.anchor: وانتصب ولوطا على الاشتغال والحكم الذي أوتيه النبوة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other interpretations take Lot’s judgment as sound adjudication between litigants or preservation of Abraham’s scriptures.
rows.anchor: وقيل: حسن الفصل بين الخصوم في القضاء. وقيل: حفظ صحف إبراهيم،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The town was Sodom; seven towns are called one because their inhabitants agreed in depravity.
rows.anchor: والقرية سدوم وكانت قراهم سبعا وعبر عنها بالواحدة لاتفاق أهلها على الفاحشة،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The towns stretched from the district of Palestine to the Sarāt and edge of the Najd in the Hijaz; God overturned six and spared Zoar, where Lot’s family and believers were.
rows.anchor: وكانت من كورة فلسطين إلى حد السراة إلى حد نجد بالحجاز، قلب منها تعالى ستا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘We rescued him from the town’s people’ means God freed Lot from them or from the punishment that struck them.
rows.anchor: أي ونجيناه من أهل القرية أي خلصناه منهم أو من العذاب الذي حل بهم،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The town is blamed figuratively for its people’s vile deeds; ‘vile deeds’ is an object meaning wicked acts, alongside disbelief and rejection of the prophet.
rows.anchor: ونسب عمل الخبائث إلى القرية مجازا وهو لأهلها وانتصب الخبائث على معنى تعمل الأعمال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording implies ‘the people of the town’; entering Lot into God’s mercy means placing him among recipients of mercy or in Paradise, which is named for mercy’s effect.
rows.anchor: وقوله إنهم يدل على أن التقدير من أهل القرية وأدخلناه في رحمتنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān calls Noah the second father of humankind after Adam, since all people descend through Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
rows.anchor: ذكر قصة أبي العالم الإنسي كلهم وهو الأب الثاني لآدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accusative Noah is governed by an understood ‘remember’; his call first summarizes his prayer as ‘I am overcome, so help me,’ then specifies his plea that no unbeliever remain on earth.
rows.anchor: وانتصب نوحا على إضمار اذكر أي واذكر نوحا أي قصته إذ نادى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-kurb is the utmost grief and constriction of breath; here it is drowning, described by its first effect on a drowning person.
rows.anchor: والكرب أقصى الغم والأخذ بالنفس، وهو هنا الغرق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author recalls reaching the bottom of the Nile and feeling such grief that death seemed near, illustrating drowning’s constriction and distress.
rows.anchor: وغَرقت في بحر النيل ووصلت إلى قرار الأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘We helped him against the people’ uses min because the verb carries the sense of rescuing or protecting him from their harm.
rows.anchor: ونصرناه من القوم عداه بمن لتضمنه معنى فنجيناه بنصرنا من القوم

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī treats naṣara as a verb whose reflexive counterpart is intaṣara and cites a Hudhaylī prayer against a thief to mean ‘make them prevail against him’; Abū Ḥayyān calls this sense non-obvious.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: هو نصر الذي مطاوعه انتصر،

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda reads min as ‘against,’ making the phrase mean that God helped Noah against the people by drowning them.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة من بمعنى على أي ونصرناه على القوم فأغرقناهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ajmaʿīn emphatically restates the object pronoun; its frequent Qur’anic use without kulluhum challenges Ibn Mālik’s claim that this is rare and usually follows kulluhum.
rows.anchor: وأجمعين تأكيد للضمير المنصوب. وقد كثر التوكيد بأجمعين

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī makes ‘when they judged’ an apposition to the mention of David and Solomon.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: وإذ بدل منهما انتهى.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān prefers understanding an omitted ‘remember’: remember David and Solomon, their story, and the case in which they judged.
rows.anchor: والأجود أن يكون التقدير واذكر داود وسليمان أي قصتهما وحالهما

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya links David and Solomon to the earlier Lot and Noah clauses under ‘We gave’; Abū Ḥayyān says this shared parse is possible.
rows.anchor: وجعل ابن عطية وداود وسليمان معطوفين على قوله ونوحا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: David was a prophet and king; the case arose when a man’s crop or vineyard was entered and damaged by another man’s sheep.
rows.anchor: وكان داود ملكا نبيا يحكم بين الناس فوقعت هذه النازلة،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: David’s grown son sat by the doorway through which litigants exited, while they entered to David through another door.
rows.anchor: وكان يجلس على الباب الذي يخرج منه الخصوم وكانوا يدخلون إلى داود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The damaged land may have been a vineyard or a field; ḥarth can mean either, though it is more commonly used for crops and less figuratively.
rows.anchor: رجل له زرع وقيل كرم والحرث يقال فيهما وهو في الزرع أكثر،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: David awarded the sheep to the crop owner: for a vineyard, their value matched the lost yield; for a field, their value matched the crop and harvest.
rows.anchor: فرأى داود دفعها إلى صاحب الحرث فعلى أنه كرم رأى أن الغنم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Solomon proposed that the sheep owner restore the field while the crop owner used the sheep’s milk, wool, and offspring; when the field recovered, each owner would receive his property back.
rows.anchor: أن يأخذ صاحب الغنم الحرث يقوم عليه ويصلحه حتى يعود كما كان،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: David praised Solomon’s judgment and ruled between the parties according to that arrangement.
rows.anchor: فقال داود: وفقت يا بني وقضى بينهما بذلك.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent view is that both David and Solomon ruled correctly according to their judgments and exercised ijtihād; this is the majority view and supports ijtihād’s permissibility.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن كلا من داود وسليمان حكم بما ظهر له وهو متوجه عنده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says each judgment came by revelation and Solomon’s abrogated David’s; ‘We made Solomon understand’ then means God gave him the final judgment He intended to establish.
rows.anchor: وقيل: حكم كل واحد منهما بوحي من الله ونسخ حكم داود بحكم سليمان

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima reads fa-afhamnāhā with a hamza; the majority reads fa-fahhamnāhā with doubled hāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عكرمة فأفهمناها عدي بالهمزة كما عدي في قراءة الجمهور بالتضعيف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in ‘We made him understand it’ refers either to the judgment or to the legal opinion.
rows.anchor: والضمير في ففهمناها للحكومة أو الفتوى.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In ‘their judgment,’ the pronoun includes judges and parties ruled for or against; the verbal noun denotes the existence of the judgment, not the act or its agent.
rows.anchor: والضمير في لحكمهم عائد على الحاكمين والمحكوم لهما وعليهما،

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reads the dual form la-ḥukmihimā, referring to David and Solomon.
rows.anchor: وقرأ لحكمهما ابن عباس فالضمير لداود وسليمان.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s being a witness means that no part of the case is hidden from Him or escapes Him.
rows.anchor: ومعنى شاهدين لا يخفى علينا منه شيء ولا يغيب.

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī explains David’s ruling by the harm caused: the sheep went to the injured owner, as in Abū Ḥanīfa’s rule for a slave who commits homicide; al-Shāfiʿī instead allows selling or ransoming the slave.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: فإن قلت: ما وجه كل واحدة من الحكومتين؟ قلت:

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī allows that the sheep’s value may have equaled the damage to the field.
rows.anchor: ولعل قيمة الغنم كانت على قدر النقصان في الحرث،

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī explains Solomon’s ruling as compensating the crop owner for lost use without transferring ownership of the sheep, while requiring the sheep owner to repair the land.
rows.anchor: ووجه حكومة سليمان أنه جعل الانتفاع بالغنم بإزاء ما فات من الانتفاع بالحرث

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Abū Ḥanīfa and his students impose no livestock liability by day or night unless an attendant was driving or leading the animal; al-Shāfiʿī requires compensation.
rows.anchor: أبو حنيفة وأصحابه لا يرون فيه ضمانا بالليل والنهار إلا أن يكون مع البهيمة سائق أو قائد،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān says both judgments were correct, citing the statement that God gave each judgment and knowledge.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن كلا من الحكمين صواب لقولهه وكلا آتينا حكما وعلما.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yusabbiḥna may be a circumstantial clause describing the mountains as praising God, or it may begin a new sentence answering how they were subjected.
rows.anchor: والظهر أن يسبحن جملة حالية من الجبال أي مسبحات.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One account says David praised God as he passed through the mountains and they answered him; another says they accompanied him wherever he went.
rows.anchor: كان يمر بالجبال مسبحا وهي تجاوبه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent view is that God created speech in the mountains so they literally praised, like the pebbles heard praising in the Prophet’s hand; Yaḥyā ibn Sallām says only David heard them, while another view says everyone did.
rows.anchor: والظاهر وقوع التسبيح منها بالنطق خلق الله فيها الكلام

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda interprets the mountains’ tasbīḥ as their praying.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة: يسبحن يصلين.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation derives yusabbiḥna from swimming or moving swiftly.
rows.anchor: وقيل: يسرن من السباحة.

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī compares the created speech to God’s speech in the tree when He spoke to Moses; Abū Ḥayyān identifies this as the Muʿtazilī denial that God truly has the attribute of speech.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: كما خلقه يعني الكلام في الشجرة حين كلم موسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A figurative view says the mountains’ movement under God’s direction led observers to attribute praise to them; most interpreters say they actually uttered ‘Glory be to God.’
rows.anchor: وقيل: إسناد التسبيح إليهن مجاز لما كانت تسير بتسيير الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accusative al-ṭayr is coordinated with the mountains, but this does not necessarily place the birds under the predicate ‘they praise.’
rows.anchor: وانتصب والطير عطفا على الجبال ولا يلزم من العطف دخوله في قيد التسبيح.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the birds are a comitative object, so they praise together with the mountains.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو مفعول معه أي يسبحن مع الطير.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A rare nominative reading makes al-ṭayr a separate topic with an omitted predicate, or coordinates it with the subject suffix in yusabbiḥna according to Kūfan grammar; the latter analysis is weak.
rows.anchor: وقرىء والطير مرفوعا على الابتداء والخبر محذوف أي مسخر

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says the mountains precede the birds because their praise is more astonishing and a clearer sign of power and miracle: they are inanimate, whereas birds are living and speaking.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: فإن قلت: لم قدمت الجبال على الطير؟ قلت:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān rejects ‘speaking’ if it means a rational soul, which would make birds human; if it means vocalizing like humans, it is inaccurate, since birds merely make sounds and are only figuratively said to speak.
rows.anchor: إن عنى به أنه ذو نفس ناطقة كما يقولون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God performs these wonders of subjugation and praise for those whom He singles out with His favor.
rows.anchor: وقوله وكنا فاعلين أي فاعلين هذه الأعاجيب من تسخير الجبال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Labūs means what is worn, in the pattern fuʿūl with a passive sense; here it means armor, though it can mean garments generally.
rows.anchor: اللبوس الملبوس فعول بمعنى مفعول كالركوب بمعنى المركوب،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An unnamed poet uses labūs for armor in a line describing lions wearing impenetrable, full coats of mail.
rows.anchor: عليها أسود ضاريات لبوسهم ... سوابغ بيض لا يخرقها النبل

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says the armor began as plates; David was the first to link them into rings, making it light and protective.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة: كانت صفائح فأول من سردها وحلقها داود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view takes labūs as all weaponry, including swords, spears, armor, and helmets, and says David first made chain mail.
rows.anchor: وقيل: اللبوس كل آلة السلاح من سيف ورمح ودرع وبيضة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says two angels criticized David for living from public funds; he prayed for a livelihood from his own work, so God softened iron for him to make armor.
rows.anchor: قيل: نزل ملكان من السماء فمرا بداود فقال أحدهما للآخر:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: By attributing the teaching of armor-making to God, the verse honors this craft as a virtue.
rows.anchor: وفي ذلك فضل هذه الصنعة إذ أسند تعليمها إياه إليه تعالى.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The armor protects people in war and provides a means of escaping the enemy.
rows.anchor: ثم امتن علينا بها بقوله لتحصنكم من بأسكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word labūs is read with a ḍamma or, by the majority, a fatḥa on its lām.
rows.anchor: وقرىء لبوس بضم اللام والجمهور بفتحها.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority reads li-yuḥṣinakum with yāʾ, making God the subject and a shift from the preceding first-person wording; Abū Bakr’s nūn reading is also cited.
rows.anchor: ليحصنكم بياء الغيبة أي الله فيكون التفاتا إذ جاء بعد ضمير متكلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Bakr transmits the nūn reading from ʿĀṣim; Abū Ḥanīfa and several others also transmit it.
rows.anchor: قراءة أبي بكر عن عاصم بالنون وهي قراءة أبي حنيفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥafṣ, al-Ḥasan, Sallām, Abū Jaʿfar, Shayba, and Zayd ibn ʿAlī read with tāʾ, making the craft or armor itself the subject.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عامر وحفص والحسن وسلام وأبو جعفر وشيبة وزيد بن علي بالتاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other transmissions read with a doubled ṣād: al-Fuqaymī and Ibn Abī Ḥammād with yāʾ, and Ibn Waththāb and al-Aʿmash with tāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الفقيمي عن أبي عمرو وابن أبي حماد عن أبي بكر بالياء من تحت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām in ‘for you’ may mark purpose and attach to ‘We taught him,’ or describe the armor; li-yuḥṣinakum may explain the teaching or the implied state of being armor for you.
rows.anchor: واللام في لكم يجوز أن تكون للتعليل فتتعلق بعلمناه،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question ‘Will you be grateful?’ implies a command to thank God for His gifts, like ‘Will you not desist?’ meaning desist from what God forbids.
rows.anchor: فهل أنتم شاكرون استفهام يتضمن الأمر أي اشكروا الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām marks the wind as placed at Solomon’s disposal, while maʿa marks the mountains’ shared accompaniment with David; the wording reflects their different relations to the prophets.
rows.anchor: وجاء التركيب هنا حين ذكر تسخير الريح لسليمان باللام، وحين ذكر تسخير الجبال جاء بلفظ مع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because David and the mountains shared praise, maʿa appropriately marks their accompaniment; the wind is assigned to Solomon because it obeyed him.
rows.anchor: وذلك أنه لما اشتركا في التسبيح ناسب ذكر مع الدالة على الاصطحاب،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readings vary: the majority has singular accusative al-rīḥ; Ibn Hurmuz and Abū Bakr transmit singular nominative; al-Ḥasan and Abū Rajāʾ plural accusative; Abū Ḥaywa plural nominative.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور الريح مفردا بالنصب. وقرأ ابن هرمز وأبو بكر في رواية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Accusative implies an omitted ‘We subjected’; nominative makes the wind a subject, and ʿāṣifa is circumstantial.
rows.anchor: فالنصب على إضمار سخرنا، والرفع على الابتداء وعاصفة حال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAṣf means force in travel, while rukāʾ means softness.
rows.anchor: والعصف الشدة في السير والرخاء اللين.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation reconciles ‘raging’ and ‘gentle’ by making them qualities at different times, according to Solomon’s need.
rows.anchor: فقيل: كان ذلك بالنسبة إلى الوقت الذي يريد فيه سليمان أحد الوصفين فلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation says the wind was gentle in itself yet forceful in its work, covering a month’s journey quickly, as another verse states.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الجمع بين الوصفين كونها رخاء في نفسها طيبة كالنسيم عاصفة في عملها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third explanation makes the wind gentle on departure and forceful on the return, following people’s habit of hurrying home; this also makes the qualities apply at different times.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الرخاء في البداءة والعصف بعد ذلك في التقول على عادة البشر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wind’s running by his command means it obeyed Solomon according to whatever he wanted and ordered.
rows.anchor: وجريها بأمره طاعتها له على حسب ما يريد، ويأمر.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The destination is identified as Syria, where Solomon lived and ruled; other views say Palestine or Jerusalem, and al-Kalbī says he rode the wind from Istakhr to Syria.
rows.anchor: والأرض أرض الشام وكانت مسكنه ومقر ملكه. وقيل: أرض فلسطين.

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī says Solomon rode the wind from Istakhr to Syria.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي كان يركب عليها من اصطخر إلى الشام.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another possibility is that any land Solomon traveled to was blessed because he established faith and justice there; the apparent syntax makes ‘which We blessed’ describe the land.
rows.anchor: قيل: ويحتمل أن تكون الأرض التي يسير إليها سليمان كائنة ما كانت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent syntax makes ‘which We blessed’ an adjective describing the land.
rows.anchor: أن التي باركنا صفة للأرض.

rows.speaker: منذر بن سعيد
rows.claim: Mundhir ibn Saʿīd says the sentence ends at ‘to the land’; ‘which We blessed’ then describes the wind, with the verse’s word order understood as rearranged.
rows.anchor: وقال منذر بن سعيد: الكلام تام عند قوله إلى الأرض

rows.speaker: وهب
rows.claim: Wahb reports that birds, jinn, and people gathered around Solomon; for campaigns a platform with people, animals, and weapons was lifted by the fierce wind and carried by the gentle wind a month each way.
rows.anchor: وعن وهب: كان سليمان إذا خرج إلى مجلسه عكفت عليه الطير

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil describes a huge gold-and-silk carpet with a gold throne, seats for prophets and scholars, people and jinn around them, birds shading Solomon, and a wind carrying it a month each way.
rows.anchor: وعن مقاتل: نسجت له الشياطين بساطا ذهبا في إبريسم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān cautions against relying on embellished chronicles about Solomon’s reign, accepting only what the Qur’an and the Prophet’s reports establish.
rows.anchor: وقد أكثر الأخباريون في ملك سليمان ولا ينبغي أن يعتمد إلا على ما قصه الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because these privileges are extraordinary, God states that His knowledge encompasses everything and events unfold according to His prior knowledge.
rows.anchor: ولما كانت هذه الاختصاصات في غاية الغرابة من المعهود، أخبر تعالى أن علمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wind is transparent and unseen while the devils are subtle, intelligent bodies; their shared quality is rapid movement, illustrated by the jinn who offers to fetch the throne before Solomon rises.
rows.anchor: ولما ذكر تعالى تسخير الريح له وهي جسم شفاف لا يعقل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preposition min before ‘the devils’ may be an object governed by ‘We subjected’ or a subject after an understood predicate; the apparent reading makes it a relative pronoun.
rows.anchor: ومن في موضع نصب أي وسخرنا من الشياطين من يغوصون

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abū al-Baqāʾ parses min as an indefinite noun qualified by a clause; the plural verb agrees with its meaning, helped by a preceding plural.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو البقاء: هي نكرة موصوفة، وجمع الضمير في يغوصون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A cited line uses feminine agreement after min because the earlier plural niswān makes the pronoun follow the meaning ‘some women,’ not the form of min.
rows.anchor: لما تقدم لفظ النسوان حمل على معنى من فأنث، ولم يقل من هو روضة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The devils dive in the sea to extract pearls; ‘diving’ itself implies both the place and the thing sought, so neither needs to be stated.
rows.anchor: والمعنى يغوصون له في البحار لاستخراج اللآلئ، ودل الغوص على المغاص فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The words ‘for him’ mean for Solomon, clarifying that the devils dove in obedience rather than for themselves.
rows.anchor: فلذلك لم يذكر أو قال له أي لسليمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reference is specifically to diving, not every kind of construction; another verse says the devils made whatever Solomon wished, including sanctuaries and statues.
rows.anchor: والإشارة بذلك إلى الغوص أي دون الغوص من بناء المدائن والقصور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report attributes bathhouses, soap, mills, glass vessels, and similar crafts to the devils’ work.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الحمام والنورة والطاحون والقوارير والصابون من استخراجهم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘We were their guardians’ may mean God kept the devils from disobeying, changing their work, or corrupting what they were made to do.
rows.anchor: وكنا لهم حافظين أي من أن يزيغوا عن أمره أو يبدلوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other explanations say God guarded people against attacks during Solomon’s time or prevented the devils from escaping.
rows.anchor: وقيل: حافظين أن يهيجوا أحدا في زمان سليمان. وقيل حافظين حتى لا يهربوا.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some say only unbelieving devils were subjected: the term ‘devils’ and the need for guardianship suggest believers would not corrupt assigned work.
rows.anchor: قيل: سخر الكفار دون المؤمنين، ويدل عليه إطلاق لفظ الشياطين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The contrast between David’s subjugated stone and iron and Solomon’s subtle wind and fiery devils displays God’s power; the demons dived in water without harm though water extinguishes fire.
rows.anchor: وتسخير أكثف الأجسام لداود وهو الحجر إذ أنطقه بالتسبيح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These wonders demonstrate that opposites can arise from opposites, resurrection of decayed bones is possible, and dry earth can become a living creature; whatever a truthful prophet reports must be believed.
rows.anchor: دليل واضح على باهر قدرته وإظهار الضد من الضد وإمكان إحياء العظم الرميم،
